title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
text:
Where you live and how much you earn are closely connected. In the United States, income is not distributed randomly across space. High-income households cluster in certain neighborhoods, low-income households cluster in others, and the boundary between them is often sharp.
Pennsylvania is a useful place to study this pattern. It contains two major metropolitan areas, Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, as well as large stretches of rural land and older industrial towns. If income is spatially concentrated, Pennsylvania should show it.
This analysis uses census tract data from the American Community Survey (ACS) to map median household income across all 3,383 tracts in Pennsylvania. A census tract is a small geographic unit, typically containing 1,200 to 8,000 people, which is small enough to reveal neighborhood-level patterns that county or city averages would hide.
The question this passage wants to answer is: where are high-income and low-income areas concentrated in Pennsylvania, and what does that pattern reveal about economic geography?
The answer turns out to be a story about scale. Income segregation appears at three levels, the state, the metropolitan area, and the neighborhood, and each level tells a different part of the story.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
text:
How I Measured It
I used data from the 2022 ACS 5-year estimates, published by the U.S. Census Bureau. The key variable is B19013_001 — median household income, in inflation-adjusted dollars.
Why median. Household income is strongly right-skewed. A small number of very high earners pull the mean far above the typical household. The median is less affected by those extreme values, so it better represents what a typical household earns.
Why census tracts. Counties and cities are too large to capture neighborhood-level variation. For example, the county-level median income hides the fact that some neighborhoods are among the wealthiest in the state while others are among the poorest. Census tracts reveal this variation with more precise division.
Data cleaning. I removed tracts with missing income estimates (62 tracts) and one tract with an empty geometry. The final sample contains 3,383 tracts, covering all 67 counties in Pennsylvania.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
section: Finding 1: Income Is Concentrated at the State Level
text:
Finding 1: Income Is Concentrated at the State Level



The geography of income in Pennsylvania


The first map shows median household income for every tract in Pennsylvania, colored by income quintile (each color contains 20% of tracts).
The pattern is clear. The lowest-income tracts (dark blue) are concentrated in: - Center City Philadelphia and its surrounding neighborhoods - Inner Pittsburgh - Older industrial towns such as Erie, Scranton, and Reading
The highest-income tracts (orange and red) are concentrated in: - Philadelphia’s western suburbs (the Main Line) - Pittsburgh’s northern and eastern suburbs - A few university towns (State College, University Park)
The middle of the state, which is the large rural area between the two metropolitan regions, is almost entirely middle-income (yellow and light blue). There are less extreme values in these regions.
What this means. Income in Pennsylvania is not evenly distributed across space. It is clustered into two main high-income zones (the Philadelphia and Pittsburgh metro areas) and a few smaller ones, surrounded by a large middle-income rural region.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
text:
Finding 2: Income Quintiles Cluster Spatially



Income quintiles cluster spatially


The second map isolates the top and bottom quintiles to make the clustering more visible.
Two patterns stand out:

High-income tracts (red) form a dense, contiguous block in southeastern Pennsylvania, stretching from Philadelphia westward into Chester and Montgomery counties. This is a large and connected region of affluence rather than a scattering of rich neighborhoods.
Low-income tracts (dark blue) also cluster, but in different places: inner Philadelphia, inner Pittsburgh, and a string of smaller cities along the Susquehanna and Lehigh rivers.

The key finding is that rich and poor tracts are adjacent to each other and form coherent geographic regions. The boundary between a red tract and a blue tract is often a single street.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
text:
Finding 3: Income Segregation Within Philadelphia



Income segregation within Philadelphia


The third map zooms into Philadelphia to show what income segregation looks like at the neighborhood level.
The pattern is striking. North Philadelphia and Kensington, which are the large sections of the city, are almost entirely dark blue (bottom quintile). Center City is light green (middle quintile, not top). Chestnut Hill and parts of South Philadelphia are orange (top quintile).
So we could make several conclusions:

Center City is not the richest part of the city. Although many tall buildings are concentrated in this economic center, many students and renters are also living in the region. so the median household income is only in the middle quintile. The wealthiest tracts are in the northwest and along the southern edge.
Low-income neighborhoods form a contiguous corridor running north from Center City. It reflects decades of disinvestment, redlining, and the geography of public housing.
High-income neighborhoods are small and separated. Unlike the poor neighborhoods, which form large continuous areas, the wealthy neighborhoods are smaller and often isolated from each other by middle-income tracts.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
text:
Conclusion
The spatial patterns in these three maps reveal three things about economic geography in Pennsylvania:
1. Income is not distributed randomly. It clusters into recognizable regions: some rich, some poor, most in between. This clustering is visible at every scale, from the whole state down to individual neighborhoods.
2. Segregation is not just about income levels. It is about spatial adjacency. A state where rich and poor neighborhoods are next to each other looks very different from a state where they are separated by large middle-income buffers. For Pennsylvania, high-income regions concentrated in the southeast and southwest, low-income regions concentrated in inner cities and older industrial towns, and a vast middle-income rural interior.
3. Scale matters. A county-level map would show Philadelphia and Pittsburgh as relatively poor and their suburbs as relatively rich. But the tract-level map shows that the story is more complicated: within Philadelphia, some neighborhoods are among the wealthiest in the state, and within the suburbs, some tracts are middle-income. Aggregation hides these patterns.
What should a reader take away? The map is not just a picture of where people live. It is a picture of opportunity — access to good schools, safe streets, and high-paying jobs is distributed unevenly across space, and the boundaries are often sharp. This is the geography that policy has to work with.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
text:
Limitations

ACS estimates are uncertain. Each tract’s median income has a margin of error, sometimes large. Small differences between adjacent tracts may not be statistically meaningful.
Median income is a crude measure. It says nothing about wealth, cost of living, or household size. A tract with many retirees may have a low median income but high wealth.
2022 snapshot. The data reflect one year. Income geography changes slowly, but the picture would differ in other years.
Tract boundaries can change. Comparisons across years require attention to boundary changes.
Spatial patterns are not causal. The maps show where income is concentrated, not why. Explanations require additional data and analysis.


Data source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates (2022), table B19013. Retrieved via the tidycensus R package. Full code and data are available in the project repository.

title: Blog3: Who Benefits Most from a College Degree?
text:
Is a college degree still worth it? This question is asked every year, but it has become more urgent as the labor market shifts. Industries that once guaranteed stable careers are shrinking, remote work has changed where and how people earn, and the cost of tuition keeps rising. For a high school student deciding whether to enroll, for a parent helping pay, and for a policymaker designing education policy, the answer matters.
The common way to answer this question is to look at the college wage premium — the gap in earnings between workers with a bachelor’s degree and workers with only a high school diploma. If the premium is large, the financial case for college is strong. If it is shrinking, the case weakens.
This analysis uses microdata from the IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS) to measure the college wage premium from 2002 to 2025, and to see how it differs across age groups and gender.
The headline result: the premium is large (around 70%) and stable overall, but it is experienced very differently by different groups. Older workers without a degree face more volatility in their earnings. Women now enjoy a larger and faster-growing premium than men. Understanding these differences matters for anyone making decisions about education, careers, or policy — and it is the central point of this post.

title: Blog3: Who Benefits Most from a College Degree?
text:
How I Measured It
I used the Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the CPS, which contains detailed annual income data for a representative sample of the U.S. population.
To make the analysis representative, I used the ASECWT sampling weight provided by IPUMS.
I restricted the sample to: - Adults aged 25–64 (prime working age) - Workers with positive earnings and hours worked - High school graduates (EDUC = 73) and bachelor’s degree holders (EDUC = 111)
All earnings are adjusted to 2010 dollars using the CPI-U, so comparisons across years are not distorted by inflation.
The college premium is defined as:
Premium = (Median earnings of bachelor's graduates
         / Median earnings of high school graduates) - 1
This research use median rather than mean earnings due to the strong right-skewed characteristic of earnings. A small number of very high earners pull the mean far above the typical worker. The median is less affected by those extreme values, so it better represents what a typical high school or college graduate earns.

title: Blog3: Who Benefits Most from a College Degree?
section: Finding 1: The Premium is in V-shaped trend
text:
Finding 1: The Premium is in V-shaped trend



The College Wage Premium, 2002–2025


The college premium rose from 60% in 2002 to 73% in 2015, then fell to 66.7% in 2022. After 2022, it rebounded to 70.5% in 2025.
One possible reason for the increasing trend before 2015 is that the premium is being drivenby the shocks to the labor market — particularly shocks that hit workers without a degree.
When low-wage jobs disappear during a recession, high school graduates’ median earnings fall, and the ratio that defines the premium mechanically rises. When those jobs recover, the premium falls back.
While the decreasing trend happened in the COVID period is another case. During the pandemic, high-paying white-collar positions are also facing the impact of layoffs and remote work. The relative demand for university graduates might weaken around 2022.

title: Blog3: Who Benefits Most from a College Degree?
section: Finding 2: The Volatility comes from high school graduates
text:
Finding 2: The Volatility comes from high school graduates



Median Earnings by Education and Age Group


To understand where the V-shape comes from, I split the sample into four age groups and plotted median earnings separately for bachelor’s and high school graduates.
The result is revealing. Bachelor’s degree holders across all four age groups have remarkably stable earnings. The blue lines in each graph move by less than 10% over 23 years, even during the financial crisis and the pandemic.
The high school lines (red) are a different story. Their earnings are more volatile, and the volatility is largest for older workers:

55–64 group: high school earnings fell from about $31,000 in 2002 to a low of about $29,000 around 2010, then recovered to roughly $33,000 by 2020, before falling back to $32,500 by 2025.
45–54 group: similar pattern, with a decline around 2010 and another dip after 2020.
25–34 and 35–44 groups: more stable, with only modest year-to-year movement.

The college premium is a ratio: bachelor’s earnings divided by high school earnings. If bachelor’s earnings are stable and high school earnings fluctuate, then the most of the movement in the premium comes from the denominator.
In this case, the premium in figure 1 did not rise because college became more valuable. It rose because high school graduates’ earnings were unusually low that period.

title: Blog3: Who Benefits Most from a College Degree?
section: Finding 3: A Persistent and Growing Gender Gap in Returns
text:
Finding 3: A Persistent and Growing Gender Gap in Returns



The College Premium by Gender, 2002–2025


The final dimension I examined is gender, and here the pattern is the most striking of all.
Women’s college premium has been higher than men’s for almost the entire period, and the gap has widened over time. What should be noticed is that a higher premium does not mean that the absolute wage of women with degrees is more than that of men with degrees. It simply means the gap between degree holders and non-degree holders is larger for women.
In 2002, the premium was 72.5% for women and 66.7% for men — a 6-point difference. By 2025, the gap had grown to more than 10 points: 85.7% for women, 75.0% for men.
The paths are also different:

Women’s premium rose steadily from 72.5% in 2002 to 85.7% in 2025 — the most consistent upward trend in the entire analysis.
Men’s premium was far more volatile. It started at 66.7%, briefly fell to 64.8% in 2007, then surged to 80.5% by 2015 — briefly overtaking women — before falling back to 75% by 2025.

The pattern is consistent with two well-documented trends in the U.S. labor market:

Women have been outpacing men in educational attainment for decades. As more women earn college degrees, the composition of the female college workforce changes, which affects measured earnings.
Male high school graduates have seen their earnings decline, particularly in manufacturing and other traditionally male-dominated industries. Female high school graduates’ earnings have been more stable (though also low, around $24,000 for most of the period).

Together, these trends mean that the college premium has become a larger advantage for women than for men — not necessarily because women’s college earnings are increasing, but because men’s alternatives have gotten worse. This partly reflects the declining fortunes of male workers without a degree.

title: Blog3: Who Benefits Most from a College Degree?
text:
Conclusion
The college wage premium remains one of the most important features of the U.S. labor market. This analysis shows it is large (around 70%) and experienced very differently across groups:

The premium is not growing steadily. Since 2015, it fell through 2022 and partially recovered by 2025. The V-shape suggests it responds to labor market shocks, not to a steady increase in the value of a degree.
Older workers without a degree face the most volatility. The 55–64 group saw high school earnings swing by $4,000 over two decades, while bachelor’s earnings barely moved. The premium moves because the alternative moves.
The gender gap in the college premium has widened. Women’s premium rose steadily to 85.7% by 2025, while men’s was more volatile and reached 75.0%. A higher premium for women does not mean higher absolute wages — it means the gap between degree and non-degree workers is larger for women.

What should a reader take away from this? The college premium is not just a measure of what a degree is worth. It is a measure of the gap between two paths — and that gap depends as much on what happens to workers without a degree as it does on what happens to workers with one. When the premium rises, it may be because college became more valuable — or because the alternative became worse. Both have happened in the U.S. over the past two decades, and both are visible in this data.

title: Blog3: Who Benefits Most from a College Degree?
text:
Limitations
This analysis has several limitations:

Descriptive, not causal. The premium measures the correlation between education and earnings. It does not prove that college causes higher earnings, since college graduates differ from non-graduates in many ways.
Median-based. The premium measures the middle of the distribution, not the full range.
Binary comparison. Only high school and bachelor’s degree holders are compared. Associate’s and graduate degrees are excluded.
Selected years. The analysis uses 7 ASEC years, not every year from 2002–2025.


Data source: IPUMS CPS, Annual Social and Economic Supplement, 2002–2025. All statistics are weighted using ASECWT. Earnings are adjusted to 2010 dollars using CPI-U. Full code and data are available in the project repository.

title: Blog1: Omitted Variable Bias — Why ‘Significant’ Isn’t Enough
text:
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together every summer. Run a simple regression of drownings on ice cream sales, and the coefficient comes out “statistically significant.” Someone could argue from that coefficient that ice cream causes drowning.
But the two are not causing each other. They are both driven by a third variable: hot weather. Hot days send people to the beach and to the ice cream truck at the same time. When that third variable is missing from the regression, the coefficient on ice cream quietly picks up weather’s effect.
This is omitted variable bias (OVB). It is one of the most common mistakes in applied economics, and it is dangerous because it does not announce itself. The coefficient looks significant, the t-statistic is large, and the model fits the data — but the estimate is wrong.
This post has two goals. First, to explain OVB clearly with a simulated example. Second, to show that the same bias appears in real data — using a large microdata sample from the IPUMS Current Population Survey. The question is simple: when we control for a variable that belongs in the model, how much does the estimated effect change?

title: Blog1: Omitted Variable Bias — Why ‘Significant’ Isn’t Enough
text:
Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together every summer. Run a simple regression of drownings on ice cream sales, and the coefficient comes out “statistically significant.” Someone could argue from that coefficient that ice cream causes drowning.

This is omitted variable bias (OVB). It is one of the most common mistakes in applied economics, and it is dangerous because it does not announce itself. The coefficient looks significant, the t-statistic is large, and the model fits the data — but the estimate is wrong.
This post has two goals. First, to explain OVB clearly with a simulated example. Second, to show that the same bias appears in real data — using a large microdata sample from the IPUMS Current Population Survey. The question is simple: when we control for a variable that belongs in the model, how much does the estimated effect change?

title: Blog1: Omitted Variable Bias — Why ‘Significant’ Isn’t Enough
section: A Tiny Demo: Ice Cream and Drowning
text:
A Tiny Demo: Ice Cream and Drowning
I generated data where weather drives both ice cream sales and drownings, and ice cream has no causal effect on drowning. Then I ran two regressions:

Model 1: drowning ~ icecream (weather omitted)
Model 2: drowning ~ icecream + temp (weather included)

The results are stark. Without weather, the ice cream coefficient is about 0.34 — large and statistically significant. Add weather, and it collapses to about −0.01, essentially zero.
The 0.34 was not ice cream’s effect on drowning. It was weather’s effect, hiding inside the ice cream variable. This is OVB in its purest form.



The ice cream coefficient disappears when weather is added



The Formula
The bias has a simple form. Suppose the truth is:
y = β₁x + β₂z + u
but you estimate y ~ x (leaving z out). The coefficient on x converges to:
β₁ + β₂ · δ,   where  δ = Cov(x, z) / Var(x)
The bias is β₂ · δ: how strongly the omitted variable affects y (β₂), times how tightly it moves with x (δ). For ice cream, both are positive, so the estimate comes out too big. And you can often predict the direction of the bias by thinking about those two signs.

title: Blog1: Omitted Variable Bias — Why ‘Significant’ Isn’t Enough
section: The Same Bias in Real Data
text:
The Same Bias in Real Data
The ice cream case is obvious. In real economic data, OVB is much harder to see.
I used microdata from the IPUMS Current Population Survey (ASEC), covering U.S. workers aged 25–64 from 2002 to 2025. The sample is restricted to high school graduates and bachelor’s degree holders. All statistics use the ASECWT sampling weight so they represent the U.S. population, not just the survey sample. Earnings are adjusted to 2010 dollars.
The question: how much does a bachelor’s degree raise earnings? This is exactly the kind of question where OVB matters, because a degree is correlated with many other things — including how many weeks a person works during the year.

What the Raw Data Looks Like



Education and earnings look strongly related


Bachelor’s degree holders clearly earn more than high school graduates. The difference is large and consistent. If you stopped here, you would conclude that education has a strong effect on earnings.


Two Models, Two Answers
I estimated two regressions, both weighted using the CPS survey design:

Model 1: log(income) ~ bachelor's degree
Model 2: log(income) ~ bachelor's degree + weeks worked

Model 1 omits weeks worked. Model 2 controls for it.



The education effect shrinks when work weeks are controlled


The result mirrors the ice cream example. Without controlling for weeks worked, the estimated return to a bachelor’s degree is 72.1%. Once weeks worked is added to the model, the estimated return falls to 64.1% — a drop of about 8 percentage points.
That 8-point gap is the bias. Part of what looked like an “education effect” was actually a “weeks worked” effect. Workers with a bachelor’s degree tend to work more weeks per year, and a model that ignores this attributes the entire earnings difference to education alone.

title: Blog1: Omitted Variable Bias — Why ‘Significant’ Isn’t Enough
text:
What This Means
The lesson is not that education has no effect. Education clearly does raise earnings — even after controlling for weeks worked, the estimated return is still 64%. The lesson is that the size of the estimated effect depends on what else is in the model, and that this is not a technicality — it changes the number you report.
Three practical takeaways:

A significant coefficient is not proof of a causal relationship. It only tells you the correlation is unlikely to be due to chance. It says nothing about whether the variable you included is the one doing the work.
Think about what is missing before you interpret a coefficient. In the ice cream case, the missing variable is obvious. In the education case, it takes more thought — but the logic is the same: what else could be driving both x and y?
The fix is usually to add the missing variable — or use a method that does not require observing it. Panel data with fixed effects, instrumental variables, and regression discontinuity are all tools for handling OVB when the omitted variable cannot be measured directly.

title: Blog1: Omitted Variable Bias — Why ‘Significant’ Isn’t Enough
text:
Conclusion
Omitted variable bias is not a rare edge case. It is the default outcome when a regression leaves out something that matters. The ice cream example makes the mechanism vivid; the CPS example shows that it affects real estimates of real economic questions.
The takeaway for a reader is this: when you see a “statistically significant” coefficient, the first question should not be “is it significant?” It should be “what is missing from this model, and which way would it push the estimate?” That question is where careful empirical work begins.

title: Blog1: Omitted Variable Bias — Why ‘Significant’ Isn’t Enough
text:
Limitations

This is a demonstration, not a causal estimate. The education regression illustrates OVB mechanics; it is not a credible estimate of the return to college. Credible estimates require panel data and careful identification.
Weeks worked is only one omitted variable. Education is correlated with many other factors (family background, ability, location, industry). Adding weeks worked reduces the bias but does not eliminate it.
The simulated example uses one random seed. The numbers shown are specific to that seed, though the qualitative pattern is stable across seeds.
CPS income data are topcoded. Very high earners are replaced with top values, which compresses the upper tail and can affect regression coefficients.


Data source: IPUMS CPS, Annual Social and Economic Supplement, 2002–2025. All statistics are weighted using ASECWT. Earnings are adjusted to 2010 dollars using CPI-U. Full code is available in the project repository.

title: Blog2: Which Technical Skills Are Most In Demand in Tech Hiring?
text:
Anyone trying to break into tech today faces the same question: what should I learn first? The answer is not obvious. There are hundreds of programming languages, frameworks, and tools, and the ones that employers ask for change from year to year. A skill that was essential five years ago may now be optional, and a tool that barely existed a decade ago may now appear in a quarter of all job postings.
This matters beyond individual career decisions. Employers use job postings to signal what they value. When those signals change, they reveal something about how the tech industry is evolving — which roles are growing, which technologies are becoming standard, and which parts of the market are pulling in different directions.
This analysis scrapes job postings from three independent sources to answer the question:
Which technical skills appear most frequently in tech job postings — and do different hiring markets demand different skills?
The answer turns out to be more complicated and depending on the market. The skills that dominate one platform are not the same skills that dominate another. That finding is the core of this post.

text:
Where the Data Comes From
I collected job postings from three different platforms, each representing a different slice of the tech hiring market:








Source
What it covers
Postings




RemoteOK
A curated remote-first job board with structured skill tags
99


We Work Remotely
A remote-only job board with detailed descriptions
25

Global startup and tech hiring, updated monthly
245



Together these sources cover a certain amount of employers and postings, such as tech companies including startups and traditional companies that hiring across onsite, hybrid, and remote arrangements.
Each platform attracts a different kind of employer, so combining them reduces the risk of drawing conclusions from a single, biased sample.

title: Blog2: Which Technical Skills Are Most In Demand in Tech Hiring?
section: The Skills That Keep Appearing in traditional tech-postings are not dominating the remote labor market
text:
The Skills That Keep Appearing in traditional tech-postings are not dominating the remote labor market
From the data, though three platforms are focusing on similar industries, the required abilities are quite different. For traditional Hacker News, Python dominates the postings.It appears in 69 of the 245 postings (28%). However, the requirement numbers for Python is other two remote platform are much lower. Especially for RemoteOK, there are only 8 postings mentioned Python in their postings.

We Work Remotely: 25 Remote Tech Postings



Skills in demand on We Work Remotely


React leads the pack, appearing in 40% of postings, followed closely by AWS and CI/CD. The pattern here points to a cloud-native, frontend-heavy skill set — exactly what you would expect from a remote-only job board. Then Docker and Python are also been noticed by several postings.


RemoteOK: 99 Remote-First Postings



Skills in demand on RemoteOK


RemoteOK’s tag data tells a different story. Go and system administration dominate, reflecting a user base of infrastructure engineers and DevOps specialists. Backend skills are more prominent here than on the other platforms.


Hacker News: 245 Global Tech Postings



Skills in demand on Hacker News

title: Blog2: Which Technical Skills Are Most In Demand in Tech Hiring?
text:
Conclusion
Across three independent sources and 369 job postings, the data does not point to a single “most in-demand” skill. Instead, it shows a segmented market:

Hacker News (startup / full-stack): Python leads at 28%, followed by TypeScript and React.
We Work Remotely (product-oriented remote companies): React leads at 40%, with AWS and CI/CD close behind.
RemoteOK (infrastructure / DevOps): Go and system administration dominate.

The broader lesson is methodological. “What skills are in demand?” sounds like a simple question, but it is not well-defined until you specify the market. Different platforms serve different employers, and the skills that matter depend on which segment you are targeting. A job seeker who looks at only one platform may draw the wrong conclusion about what to learn — and a researcher who looks at only one platform may draw the wrong conclusion about what the tech industry values.

What This Analysis Cannot Tell You
A few honest limitations:

It is a snapshot. The data was collected in September 2026 and reflects one moment in a fast-moving market.
Job postings are not hires. Employers list many skills they never actually test for. Advertised demand is a rough proxy for real demand.
Keyword counting is imprecise. A posting that mentions “Python” once counts the same as one that mentions it ten times.

These limitations do not undermine the findings — the patterns are strong enough to be meaningful — but they are worth keeping in mind.

title: Blog4: Does Population Growth Bring Prosperity?
text:
Every year, hundreds of thousands of Americans move between states. They leave the Northeast and Midwest for the Sun Belt, chasing lower taxes, cheaper housing, and new job opportunities. Meanwhile, there are also immigrants from foreign countries entering different states. Their choice also includes consideration to their new life condition. Between 2000 and 2025, Nevada’s population grew by 63%, Utah’s by 58%, and Texas’s by 51%. Meanwhile, West Virginia lost population, and Illinois barely grew at all.
This migration is not just a demographic fact. It is often treated as a signal of economic success. States that attract new residents are said to be “winning” — they have jobs, opportunities, and a future. States that lose residents are said to be “declining.”
But is that true? Does population growth actually mean that the people living in a state are becoming richer? Or are migrants moving to places that are cheaper — not necessarily more prosperous?
This analysis uses data from the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) system to examine population and income trends across all 50 U.S. states (plus D.C.) from 2000 to 2025. The data is retrieved programmatically through the fredr R package, so the entire analysis is reproducible.
The answer, it turns out, is more nuanced than the headline numbers suggest. Population growth and income growth are two different things — and confusing them can lead to the wrong conclusions about which states are doing well.

title: Blog4: Does Population Growth Bring Prosperity?
text:
How to measure
I used two annual series for each state:

Population ({state}POP) — resident population in thousands
Per capita personal income ({state}PCPI) — total personal income divided by population, in current dollars

Using per capita income is essential when comparing states of different sizes.
All figures are in current (nominal) dollars. Real growth after inflation would be lower; this is discussed in the Limitations.
I collected data for all 51 jurisdictions (50 states plus the District of Columbia) from 2000 through 2025 — about 2,652 observations in total.

title: Blog4: Does Population Growth Bring Prosperity?
section: Finding 1: Growth Is Concentrated in the West and South
text:
Finding 1: Growth Is Concentrated in the West and South



Top states by population growth


The fastest-growing states are all in the West and South: Nevada (+63%), Utah (+58%), Idaho (+56%), Texas (+51%), Arizona (+48%), and Florida (+46%).



Bottom states by population growth


The slowest-growing states are all in the Midwest and Northeast: West Virginia (-2.3%), Michigan (+1.8%), Illinois (+2.3%), Louisiana (+3.3%), and Mississippi (+3.7%).
West Virginia is the only state that lost population over the period. This is consistent with long-running trend of out-migration of young workers, declining coal employment, and an aging population in that area.

title: Blog4: Does Population Growth Bring Prosperity?
section: Finding 2: Population Growth Does Not Mean Income Growth
text:
Finding 2: Population Growth Does Not Mean Income Growth



Population growth vs. income growth


If population growth were a sign of economic success, we would expect the fastest-growing states to also show the fastest income growth. However, the data shows no such relationship. According to the scatter plot, it shows only a weak, noisy-positive relationship.
For example: Nevada has a population growth of 63%, which is the highest in the country, but has a nominal income growth of only 135%. Meanwhile, Utah has a similar population growth of 58%, but Utah’s nominal per capita income grew roughly 190% versus Nevada’s 135%. In this case, the relationship between income and population growth is relatively week.

title: Blog4: Does Population Growth Bring Prosperity?
section: Finding 3: Income Growth Differ More Among Slow-Growing States
text:
Finding 3: Income Growth Differ More Among Slow-Growing States



Income trajectories by growth group


Then, we collected the income growth data for the six fastest-growing states and the six slowest-growing states in terms of population growth.
Among population-fast-growing states, per capita income range is relatively narrow: all six states end the period between $65,000 and $77,000.
Among population-slow-growing states, the range is much wider: Illinois reaches nearly $80,000 by 2025, while Mississippi remains near $55,000.
In this case, Population growth is not a signal of prosperity, but population stagnation is not a signal of decline either. Illinois has one of the highest per capita incomes in the country while its population has remained roughly flat.The reason is that both population inflow and outflow exist in each state. If a state is attracting high-skilled immigrants while those leaving the state were the middle and low-income locals, the income per capita for the state would increase while population would remain stable.

title: Blog4: Does Population Growth Bring Prosperity?
text:
Conclusion
This analysis leads to three takeaways:

Population growth is not a reliable indicator of income growth. Nevada and Utah both grew quickly, but their income growth was very different. Meanwhile, Illinois’s population remained flat while its per capita income grew steadily.
Income growth is not driven by the net change in population. The two variables are only weakly correlated. The people who leave a state and the people who arrive are different in income, skills, and consumption behavior. As a result, income is affected by who is in the population, not just how many people there are.
The composition of migration matters more than the headline number. A state can grow quickly and remain poor, or stagnate and remain rich. The interesting question is not “how many people moved in?” but “who moved in, and who moved out?”

What should a reader take away from this? If you are deciding where to live, do not assume that population fast-growing states are richer or that population slow-growing states are declining. The two are only loosely connected. Population change is a useful signal, but it is not the same as economic prosperity.

title: Blog4: Does Population Growth Bring Prosperity?
text:
Limitations
This analysis has several limitations:

Per capita income is a crude measure. It divides total income by total population, including children and retirees who do not earn income.
No inflation and cost-of-living adjustment. The analysis use nominal income data so the growth rates reported here include both real income growth and price inflation. Meanwhile, a dollar in Mississippi buys more than a dollar in California, but this analysis treats them as equal.
Population estimates, not census counts. FRED uses annual estimates between decennial censuses, which can diverge from actual counts.
Simple correlation. The analysis describes patterns, not causes. It does not explain why some states grow and others do not.
Population growth combines natural increase and net migration. This analysis cannot separate the two, so statements about migration specifically are not supported.


Data source: FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. State population ({state}POP) and per capita personal income ({state}PCPI), 2000–2025. All data retrieved programmatically through the fredr R package. Full code is available in the project repository.

title: Blog6: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
How much of our economic success is determined by our parents? Economists measure this using the Intergenerational Elasticity (IGE) — a metric that captures how a percentage change in parents’ income affects their children’s income.
Estimating this requires matching parents to their children across time. In longitudinal datasets like the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), this is a complex data engineering task. You cannot simply look at a single row; you have to track individuals across decades and link families together using unique identifiers.
In this tutorial, I will demonstrate how to use SQL within Python to construct this parent-child match. We will use a real dataset from the PSID, which has been pre-matched using the Family Identification Mapping System (FIMS).
By the end of this tutorial, you will know how to: 1. Load a longitudinal dataset into a SQL database using Python. 2. Use SELECT and JOIN to match parents and children using individual IDs. 3. Use GROUP BY to compare income across subgroups. 4. Estimate the IGE and understand why averaging income over multiple years avoids the life-cycle bias.

section: Step 1: Set Up Your Python Environment
text:
Step 1: Set Up Your Python Environment
You will need Python installed (version 3.7 or higher). We will use pandas to handle data, pandasql to run SQL directly on pandas DataFrames, and statsmodels to run our regression.
In your Python terminal, install the necessary packages:
pip install pandas pandasql statsmodels
Now, import the libraries in your Python script or Jupyter Notebook:
import pandas as pd
import pandasql as ps
import statsmodels.api as sm

title: Blog6: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
section: Step 2: Load the Real PSID Data
text:
Step 2: Load the Real PSID Data
We use the ICPSR “Class exercise: Predicting income mobility in PSID” dataset. This dataset contains three generations (g1, g2, g3). The income variables are already averaged over multiple years (to adjust for life-cycle bias) and logged.
(Make sure learning.csv is in your working directory)
# Load the dataset
df = pd.read_csv("learning.csv")

# Inspect the first few rows
print(df.head())
What the variables mean: - g2_id: The parent’s unique identifier. - g3_id: The child’s unique identifier. - g2_log_income: The parent’s average log income. - g3_log_income: The child’s average log income. - g2_educ, g3_educ: Educational attainment. - sex, race: Demographic controls.

title: Blog6: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
section: Step 3: SQL Step 1 - Creating Tables and JOINing
text:
Step 3: SQL Step 1 - Creating Tables and JOINing
In real-world data engineering, parents and children might be stored in separate tables. We can simulate this by splitting our DataFrame, and then using SQL’s JOIN to bring them back together.
# Split the data into "Parent" and "Child" tables
parents = df[['g2_id', 'g2_log_income', 'g2_educ']]
children = df[['g3_id', 'g2_id', 'g3_log_income', 'g3_educ', 'sex', 'race']]

# Use SQL to JOIN them back together
query_join = """
    SELECT 
        c.g3_id,
        c.g2_id,
        c.g3_log_income,
        c.g3_educ,
        c.sex,
        c.race,
        p.g2_log_income,
        p.g2_educ
    FROM children c
    JOIN parents p ON c.g2_id = p.g2_id
"""

# Run the SQL query using pandasql
family_matched = ps.sqldf(query_join, locals())

# Remove exact duplicates that may arise from multi-child households
family_matched = family_matched.drop_duplicates()

print(f"Total matched children: {len(family_matched)}")
print(family_matched.head())
Explanation: The JOIN statement combines rows from children and parents where the g2_id (Parent ID) matches. This is the core of the parent-child match.

title: Blog6: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
section: Step 4: SQL Step 2 - GROUP BY and Aggregation
text:
Step 4: SQL Step 2 - GROUP BY and Aggregation
We can use SQL’s GROUP BY and aggregation functions (like COUNT and AVG) to explore differences in income across demographic groups.
Let’s compare the average log income of parents and children by sex:
query_group = """
    SELECT 
        sex,
        COUNT(g3_id) AS sample_size,
        AVG(g2_log_income) AS avg_parent_income,
        AVG(g3_log_income) AS avg_child_income
    FROM family_matched
    GROUP BY sex
"""

grouped_income = ps.sqldf(query_group, locals())
print(grouped_income)

title: Blog6: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Step 5: Why Averaging Matters (Life-Cycle Bias)
A crucial concept in intergenerational mobility is life-cycle bias.
If we use a parent’s income from a single year (e.g., when they are 25, just starting their career), we underestimate their “permanent” economic status. If we use a single year when they are 65 (retired), we also get a distorted picture.
To fix this, the PSID dataset we are using has already calculated g2_log_income and g3_log_income as multi-year averages (specifically, averaged over ages 30-45).
In a raw panel dataset, you would use SQL to do this:
-- Example of how averaging is done in SQL
SELECT parent_id, AVG(income) as avg_income
FROM income_table
WHERE age BETWEEN 30 AND 45
GROUP BY parent_id;
By averaging, we smooth out temporary shocks (like a brief unemployment spell) and measure permanent income. This significantly improves the accuracy of our IGE estimates.

title: Blog6: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Step 6: Estimating the IGE
Now we estimate the IGE using the matched data. The OLS regression is: [ (Income_{child}) = _0 + 1 (Income{parent}) + ]
# Extract variables
X = family_matched['g2_log_income']
y = family_matched['g3_log_income']

# Add a constant (intercept)
X = sm.add_constant(X)

# Fit OLS model
model = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()

# Print summary
print(model.summary())
Interpreting the results: Looking at the output, the coefficient on g2_log_income is 0.545 and highly significant ((p < 0.01)).
This means the Intergenerational Elasticity is 0.545. A 10% increase in a parent’s permanent income is associated with a 5.45% increase in their child’s income. This high elasticity indicates that economic advantages (and disadvantages) are strongly transmitted from parents to children in the U.S.

title: Blog6: Matching Parents and Children with SQL in Python
text:
Conclusion
In this tutorial, we successfully used SQL within Python to:

Load real PSID data.
Use JOIN to match parent and child tables using individual identifiers.
Use GROUP BY to aggregate income by demographic groups.
Estimate an IGE of 0.545 using multi-year averaged income.

By understanding how SQL can manipulate longitudinal data, and why averaging over multiple years is necessary to combat life-cycle bias, we can build robust models of intergenerational mobility.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
text:
Where you live and how much you earn are closely connected. In the United States, income is not distributed randomly across space. High-income households cluster in certain neighborhoods, low-income households cluster in others, and the boundary between them is often sharp.
Pennsylvania is a useful place to study this pattern. It contains two major metropolitan areas, Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, as well as large stretches of rural land and older industrial towns. If income is spatially concentrated, Pennsylvania should show it.
This analysis uses census tract data from the American Community Survey (ACS) to map median household income across all 3,383 tracts in Pennsylvania. A census tract is a small geographic unit, typically containing 1,200 to 8,000 people, which is small enough to reveal neighborhood-level patterns that county or city averages would hide.
The question this passage wants to answer is: where are high-income and low-income areas concentrated in Pennsylvania, and what does that pattern reveal about economic geography?
The answer turns out to be a story about scale. Income segregation appears at three levels, the state, the metropolitan area, and the neighborhood, and each level tells a different part of the story.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
text:
How I Measured It
I used data from the 2022 ACS 5-year estimates, published by the U.S. Census Bureau. The key variable is B19013_001 — median household income, in inflation-adjusted dollars.
Why median. Household income is strongly right-skewed. A small number of very high earners pull the mean far above the typical household. The median is less affected by those extreme values, so it better represents what a typical household earns.
Why census tracts. Counties and cities are too large to capture neighborhood-level variation. For example, the county-level median income hides the fact that some neighborhoods are among the wealthiest in the state while others are among the poorest. Census tracts reveal this variation with more precise division.
Data cleaning. I removed tracts with missing income estimates (62 tracts) and one tract with an empty geometry. The final sample contains 3,383 tracts, covering all 67 counties in Pennsylvania.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
section: Finding 1: Income Is Concentrated at the State Level
text:
Finding 1: Income Is Concentrated at the State Level



The geography of income in Pennsylvania


The first map shows median household income for every tract in Pennsylvania, colored by income quintile (each color contains 20% of tracts).
The pattern is clear. The lowest-income tracts (dark blue) are concentrated in: - Center City Philadelphia and its surrounding neighborhoods - Inner Pittsburgh - Older industrial towns such as Erie, Scranton, and Reading
The highest-income tracts (orange and red) are concentrated in: - Philadelphia’s western suburbs (the Main Line) - Pittsburgh’s northern and eastern suburbs - A few university towns (State College, University Park)
The middle of the state, which is the large rural area between the two metropolitan regions, is almost entirely middle-income (yellow and light blue). There are less extreme values in these regions.
What this means. Income in Pennsylvania is not evenly distributed across space. It is clustered into two main high-income zones (the Philadelphia and Pittsburgh metro areas) and a few smaller ones, surrounded by a large middle-income rural region.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
text:
Finding 2: Income Quintiles Cluster Spatially



Income quintiles cluster spatially


The second map isolates the top and bottom quintiles to make the clustering more visible.
Two patterns stand out:

High-income tracts (red) form a dense, contiguous block in southeastern Pennsylvania, stretching from Philadelphia westward into Chester and Montgomery counties. This is a large and connected region of affluence rather than a scattering of rich neighborhoods.
Low-income tracts (dark blue) also cluster, but in different places: inner Philadelphia, inner Pittsburgh, and a string of smaller cities along the Susquehanna and Lehigh rivers.

The key finding is that rich and poor tracts are adjacent to each other and form coherent geographic regions. The boundary between a red tract and a blue tract is often a single street.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
text:
Finding 3: Income Segregation Within Philadelphia



Income segregation within Philadelphia


The third map zooms into Philadelphia to show what income segregation looks like at the neighborhood level.
The pattern is striking. North Philadelphia and Kensington, which are the large sections of the city, are almost entirely dark blue (bottom quintile). Center City is light green (middle quintile, not top). Chestnut Hill and parts of South Philadelphia are orange (top quintile).
So we could make several conclusions:

Center City is not the richest part of the city. Although many tall buildings are concentrated in this economic center, many students and renters are also living in the region. so the median household income is only in the middle quintile. The wealthiest tracts are in the northwest and along the southern edge.
Low-income neighborhoods form a contiguous corridor running north from Center City. It reflects decades of disinvestment, redlining, and the geography of public housing.
High-income neighborhoods are small and separated. Unlike the poor neighborhoods, which form large continuous areas, the wealthy neighborhoods are smaller and often isolated from each other by middle-income tracts.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
text:
Conclusion
The spatial patterns in these three maps reveal three things about economic geography in Pennsylvania:
1. Income is not distributed randomly. It clusters into recognizable regions: some rich, some poor, most in between. This clustering is visible at every scale, from the whole state down to individual neighborhoods.
2. Segregation is not just about income levels. It is about spatial adjacency. A state where rich and poor neighborhoods are next to each other looks very different from a state where they are separated by large middle-income buffers. For Pennsylvania, high-income regions concentrated in the southeast and southwest, low-income regions concentrated in inner cities and older industrial towns, and a vast middle-income rural interior.
3. Scale matters. A county-level map would show Philadelphia and Pittsburgh as relatively poor and their suburbs as relatively rich. But the tract-level map shows that the story is more complicated: within Philadelphia, some neighborhoods are among the wealthiest in the state, and within the suburbs, some tracts are middle-income. Aggregation hides these patterns.
What should a reader take away? The map is not just a picture of where people live. It is a picture of opportunity — access to good schools, safe streets, and high-paying jobs is distributed unevenly across space, and the boundaries are often sharp. This is the geography that policy has to work with.

title: Blog5: The Geography of Income in Pennsylvania
text:
Limitations

ACS estimates are uncertain. Each tract’s median income has a margin of error, sometimes large. Small differences between adjacent tracts may not be statistically meaningful.
Median income is a crude measure. It says nothing about wealth, cost of living, or household size. A tract with many retirees may have a low median income but high wealth.
2022 snapshot. The data reflect one year. Income geography changes slowly, but the picture would differ in other years.
Tract boundaries can change. Comparisons across years require attention to boundary changes.
Spatial patterns are not causal. The maps show where income is concentrated, not why. Explanations require additional data and analysis.


Data source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates (2022), table B19013. Retrieved via the tidycensus R package. Full code and data are available in the project repository.

title: Blog7: Interactive Visualization of the College Wage Premium
text:
In my previous analysis (Blog 3), I examined the College Wage Premium — the percentage gap in median earnings between bachelor’s degree holders and high school graduates. Using static line charts, I found that the aggregate premium followed a V-shaped trend: rising until 2015, falling during the pandemic, and partially recovering.
However, a static chart of multiple age groups had a major limitation: when four lines overlap, cross, and spike simultaneously, the human eye cannot track them. In Blog 3, I could only conclude that “older workers face more volatility,” but I couldn’t pinpoint exactly when and how much each group spiked.
This is where interactive data visualization becomes indispensable. In this post, I use the plotly library in R to rebuild the same dataset. By comparing the interactive chart to the static chart in Blog 3, I will show how interactivity adds substantive value, revealing macroeconomic shocks that were hidden in plain sight.

The Data and Methodology
I reconstructed the dataset from raw IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS) microdata, covering U.S. workers aged 25–64 from 2002 to 2025.

Cleaning: Filtered for positive wage income, restricted education levels to high school (EDUC = 73) and bachelor’s degrees (EDUC = 111).

library(plotly)

    color = ~age_group,

The Interactive Visualization

title: Blog7: Interactive Visualization of the College Wage Premium
section: Why Interactivity Matters: Static vs. Interactive
text:
Why Interactivity Matters: Static vs. Interactive
In Blog 3, I used a static ggplot. Looking at that static image, the four lines crossed so frequently that it was impossible to track the exact value of one group without losing sight of the others.
The Plotly interactive chart fundamentally changes how we read the story:

1. Zooming into Economic Shocks
In the static chart, the lines for 2007–2010 and 2019–2022 looked like chaotic zig-zags. With Plotly’s zoom feature, we can isolate these periods. By zooming into 2022, we can clearly see that the 45-54 and 55-64 age groups both spiked to over 80%, while the 25-34 group stayed flat around 66%. This specific divergence was hidden in the static graph.


2. Isolating Specific Cohorts
In Blog 3, I concluded that “older workers face more volatility.” But with the interactive legend, we can test this. Clicking on 25-34 hides the other lines, revealing a sharp plunge to 60% during the 2007 financial crisis. Clicking on 55-64 shows a completely different trajectory: a slow decline until 2019, followed by a massive pandemic spike. The interactive tool proves that the “volatility” was not a generic trend, but a series of distinct, age-specific shocks.


3. Unified Hovering
The hovermode = "x unified" setting allows a reader to place their mouse on 2015 and instantly see all four premiums: 25-34 (74.5%), 35-44 (76.5%), 45-54 (76.5%), and 55-64 (66.7%). In a static chart, comparing four points visually requires tracing invisible horizontal lines with your eyes. Plotly removes this cognitive burden.

title: Blog7: Interactive Visualization of the College Wage Premium
text:
Key Findings (Revisiting Blog 3)
By utilizing the interactive features, we uncover a story that was obscured in the static charts of Blog 3:

The aggregate trend masks severe internal volatility. While Blog 3 showed a smooth V-shape for the overall economy, the interactive chart reveals that each age group experienced entirely different cycles.
The 2022 spike was driven by older workers. The interactive hover reveals that in 2022, the 45-54 and 55-64 groups jumped to 82.5%, while younger groups remained stable. This suggests pandemic-era labor shortages disproportionately boosted the relative premium of older, experienced workers.
Frequent crossovers mean there is no “permanent” winning cohort. The lines for 45-54 and 55-64 cross multiple times. The relative advantage of a degree fluctuates wildly depending on macroeconomic timing, not just age.

title: Blog7: Interactive Visualization of the College Wage Premium
text:
Conclusion
Interactive visualization is not just a cosmetic upgrade to static charts. As demonstrated by comparing this Plotly graph to the static charts in Blog 3, interactivity transforms the reader’s relationship with the data. It shifts the analysis from “passive viewing” to “active exploration.”
For messy, overlapping macroeconomic data, a static chart forces the reader to accept the author’s narrative. An interactive chart allows the reader to find their own. By zooming into 2022, isolating the 2007 crash, or hovering to compare exact values, readers can uncover the age-specific shocks that make the U.S. labor market so complex.

Data source: IPUMS CPS, Annual Social and Economic Supplement, 2002–2025. Weighted using ASECWT. Earnings in 2010 dollars.

title: Blog8: Simulation and Statistical Inference
text:
Statistical inference is the process of drawing conclusions about a population based on a sample. But how do we know how much confidence to place in those conclusions?
Formulas like standard errors and p-values are powerful, but they often feel like magic black boxes. To truly understand them, this post uses Monte Carlo simulation to visualize three foundational concepts in statistics: 1. How a Bootstrap Confidence Interval is constructed. 2. What it actually means for a 95% Confidence Interval to have 95% coverage. 3. How Hypothesis Testing and p-values work by simulating a null distribution.
To make these concepts intuitive, I built an interactive Shiny App in R. The complete code is provided at the end of this post.

text:

To truly understand them, this post uses Monte Carlo simulation to visualize three foundational concepts in statistics: 1. How a Bootstrap Confidence Interval is constructed. 2. What it actually means for a 95% Confidence Interval to have 95% coverage. 3. How Hypothesis Testing and p-values work by simulating a null distribution.
To make these concepts intuitive, I built an interactive Shiny App in R. The complete code is provided at the end of this post.

title: Blog8: Simulation and Statistical Inference
text:
The Setup: A Known Population
To verify our statistical methods, we first need a “truth.” The simulation below assumes a population that follows a normal distribution with a true mean ((= 100)) and a standard deviation ((= 15)).
The goal of inference is to see if we can recover (= 100) using only a small sample.

title: Blog8: Simulation and Statistical Inference
text:
Part 1: The Bootstrap Confidence Interval
If we don’t know the theoretical distribution of our data, how do we calculate a confidence interval? We use the Bootstrap.
The logic is simple: if the sample is a good representation of the population, we can treat the sample as the population. We draw thousands of “resamples” from our original sample (with replacement) and calculate the mean of each resample.
The interactive chart below shows the distribution of 1,000 bootstrap means drawn from a single sample of size (n=50).



Interactive Bootstrap Distribution


How to read the chart: - The black solid line is the true population mean ((= 100)). - The light blue histogram is the distribution of our 1,000 resampled means. - The red dashed lines represent the 95% Confidence Interval. We find these by taking the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap distribution.
In the Shiny App, you can change the Confidence Level to 80% (the red lines will move closer together) or increase the number of simulations (the histogram will become smoother).

title: Blog8: Simulation and Statistical Inference
section: Part 2: What does “95% Confidence” actually mean?
text:
Part 2: What does “95% Confidence” actually mean?
Many people mistakenly believe that a 95% confidence interval means “there is a 95% chance that the true mean is inside this specific interval.” This is mathematically incorrect.
The true meaning of frequentist confidence is about long-run coverage. If we repeated our experiment 100 times, drew 100 different samples, and calculated 100 different confidence intervals, we would expect about 95 of those intervals to contain the true mean.
The chart below simulates exactly this. It runs 100 different trials, each with its own sample and confidence interval.



Confidence Interval Coverage


How to read the chart: - Each horizontal line represents one experiment. - Green lines are intervals that successfully captured the true mean (100). - Red lines are the “failures” — intervals that missed the true mean. - The dashed black line is the true mean.
Because we are using a 95% confidence level, exactly 95 of the lines should be green, and 5 should be red. In the Shiny App, you can change the Confidence Level to 80%; you will immediately see more red lines (20 out of 100).

title: Blog8: Simulation and Statistical Inference
text:
Part 3: Hypothesis Testing and P-values
Finally, let’s look at hypothesis testing. Suppose our null hypothesis is (H_0: = 100). We want to know if our sample provides enough evidence to reject (H_0).
To do this, we simulate the Null Distribution. We generate thousands of fake datasets assuming the null hypothesis is true (i.e., (= 100)), calculate a T-statistic for each, and plot the resulting distribution.



Hypothesis Testing


How to read the chart: - The light gray histogram is the distribution of T-statistics under the null hypothesis. - The red vertical line is the T-statistic we actually observed from our sample. - The p-value is the probability of getting a T-statistic as extreme as our red line, assuming the null hypothesis is true. Visually, it is the area under the curve to the right of the red line.
If the red line is far into the tail of the distribution, the p-value is small, and we reject the null hypothesis.

title: Blog8: Simulation and Statistical Inference
text:
Conclusion
Simulation strips away the mystery of statistical inference.

Bootstrap shows us how to construct confidence intervals without assuming a theoretical distribution.
Coverage simulations prove that a 95% confidence interval is a property of the procedure, not a single interval.
Null distributions make p-values visual, showing exactly how rare our observed data would be if the null hypothesis were true.

title: Blog8: Simulation and Statistical Inference
text:
Appendix: Interactive Shiny App Code
Below is the complete R code for the interactive Shiny application. If you have R installed, you can run this code locally to explore how changing the sample size, number of simulations, and confidence level affects the results.

library(shiny)
library(plotly)
library(tidyverse)

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Interactive Statistical Inference Demo"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      sliderInput("n", "Sample Size (n):", min = 10, max = 200, value = 50),
      sliderInput("sims", "Number of Bootstrap Simulations:", min = 100, max = 2000, value = 1000, step = 100),
      sliderInput("conf", "Confidence Level:", min = 0.80, max = 0.99, value = 0.95, step = 0.01),
      actionButton("resample", "Draw New Sample")
    ),
    mainPanel(
      tabsetPanel(
        tabPanel("1. Bootstrap Distribution", plotlyOutput("boot_plot")),
        tabPanel("2. CI Coverage (Simulations)", plotlyOutput("coverage_plot")),
        tabPanel("3. Hypothesis Testing", plotlyOutput("test_plot"))
      )
    )
  )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  true_mean <- 100
  true_sd <- 15
  
  sample_data <- eventReactive(input$resample, {
    rnorm(input$n, mean = true_mean, sd = true_sd)
  }, ignoreNULL = FALSE)
  
  output$boot_plot <- renderPlotly({
    data <- sample_data()
    boot_means <- replicate(input$sims, mean(sample(data, replace = TRUE)))
    alpha <- (1 - input$conf) / 2
    ci <- quantile(boot_means, probs = c(alpha, 1 - alpha))
    df <- data.frame(boot_means = boot_means)
    
    p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = boot_means)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "skyblue", color = "white") +
      geom_vline(xintercept = ci[1], color = "red", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = ci[2], color = "red", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = true_mean, color = "black", size = 1.5) +
      labs(title = "Bootstrap Distribution of the Mean",
           subtitle = paste("True Mean vs ", input$conf*100, "% CI"),
           x = "Bootstrap Sample Means", y = "Frequency") +
      theme_minimal()
    ggplotly(p)
  })
  
  output$coverage_plot <- renderPlotly({
    trials <- 100
    ci_df <- data.frame(trial = 1:trials, lower = numeric(trials), upper = numeric(trials), covers = logical(trials))
    alpha <- (1 - input$conf) / 2
    
    for(i in 1:trials) {
      x <- rnorm(input$n, mean = true_mean, sd = true_sd)
      m <- mean(x)
      se <- sd(x) / sqrt(input$n)
      z <- qnorm(1 - alpha)
      ci_df$lower[i] <- m - z * se
      ci_df$upper[i] <- m + z * se
      ci_df$covers[i] <- (true_mean >= ci_df$lower[i]) & (true_mean <= ci_df$upper[i])
    }
    
    p <- ggplot(ci_df, aes(x = trial, ymin = lower, ymax = upper, color = covers)) +
      geom_linerange(size = 1) +
      geom_hline(yintercept = true_mean, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", size = 1) +
      scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "green", "FALSE" = "red"), guide = "none") +
      labs(title = "Coverage of Confidence Intervals",
           x = "Simulation Trial", y = "Confidence Interval") +
      theme_minimal()
    ggplotly(p)
  })
  
  output$test_plot <- renderPlotly({
    x <- sample_data()
    obs_t <- (mean(x) - true_mean) / (sd(x) / sqrt(input$n))
    null_t <- replicate(input$sims, {
      x_null <- rnorm(input$n, mean = true_mean, sd = true_sd)
      (mean(x_null) - true_mean) / (sd(x_null) / sqrt(input$n))
    })
    df <- data.frame(null_t = null_t)
    
    p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = null_t)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "lightgray", color = "white", aes(y = ..density..)) +
      stat_function(fun = dnorm, color = "blue", size = 1) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = obs_t, color = "red", size = 1.5) +
      labs(title = "Null Distribution and P-value",
           x = "T-statistic", y = "Density") +
      theme_minimal()
    ggplotly(p)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

title: Blog10: Can Machine Learning Predict Poverty?
text:
Poverty is a persistent feature of the U.S. labor market, affecting roughly 11% of adults in any given year. While economists have long studied the structural drivers of poverty—such as education and employment status—less attention has been paid to whether we can predict who is at risk at the individual level. Accurate prediction is practically useful: it allows social safety net programs to proactively target resources to those who need them most.
This analysis uses microdata from the IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS) to build a complete machine learning workflow. I compare a simple logistic regression benchmark against Random Forest and XGBoost to predict whether an adult falls below the official poverty line.
The headline result: Machine learning offers a modest but meaningful improvement over the baseline, and its true value lies in targeting. By identifying the top 20% highest-risk individuals, the model locates a subgroup where the poverty rate is 25.4%—more than double the national average of 10.4%.

title: Blog10: Can Machine Learning Predict Poverty?
text:
Poverty is a persistent feature of the U.S. labor market, affecting roughly 11% of adults in any given year. While economists have long studied the structural drivers of poverty—such as education and employment status—less attention has been paid to whether we can predict who is at risk at the individual level. Accurate prediction is practically useful: it allows social safety net programs to proactively target resources to those who need them most.
This analysis uses microdata from the IPUMS Current Population Survey (CPS) to build a complete machine learning workflow. I compare a simple logistic regression benchmark against Random Forest and XGBoost to predict whether an adult falls below the official poverty line.
The headline result: Machine learning offers a modest but meaningful improvement over the baseline, and its true value lies in targeting. By identifying the top 20% highest-risk individuals, the model locates a subgroup where the poverty rate is 25.4%—more than double the national average of 10.4%.

title: Blog10: Can Machine Learning Predict Poverty?
text:
How I Measured It
I used the 2024 Annual Social and Economic Supplement (ASEC) of the CPS, which contains detailed annual income and demographic data.
To avoid data leakage, I strictly excluded current wage income (INCWAGE) since the poverty line is mechanically defined by income. The predictors include: - Age (AGE) - Sex (SEX) - Education, binned into three groups: high school or less, some college, and bachelor’s plus. - Employment status, binned into three groups: employed, unemployed, and not in the labor force.
The data is split 80/20 into training and test sets. Because the poverty rate is only 10.4%, accuracy is a misleading metric (a naive model predicting “no poverty” for everyone would be 89.6% accurate). Instead, I evaluate models primarily using ROC-AUC and a targeted policy metric: the actual poverty rate within the 20% of individuals assigned the highest predicted risk.
I compare three models: Logistic Regression (Baseline), Random Forest, and XGBoost. Hyperparameters for the tree models are tuned using cross-validation on the training set, ensuring the test set remains completely unseen until final evaluation.

The results reveal that machine learning offers a modest but real improvement over the baseline. The logistic regression performs surprisingly well, achieving an AUC of 0.740. However, the gradient boosting model (XGBoost) outperforms it, reaching an AUC of 0.765.
The more practical metric is the “Targeting” performance. While the overall poverty rate in the test set is 10.4%, the 20% of individuals with the highest predicted risk from XGBoost have an actual poverty rate of 25.4%. For a policymaker, this means ML can sharply focus limited resources on the most vulnerable groups instead of random selection.

title: Blog10: Can Machine Learning Predict Poverty?
section: Finding 2: Labor Force Detachment is the Biggest Risk
text:
Finding 2: Labor Force Detachment is the Biggest Risk



XGBoost SHAP values: Drivers of Poverty Risk


To understand what the XGBoost model learned, I compute SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values on the test set. SHAP values decompose each individual’s prediction, showing how much each feature pushed the predicted probability of poverty up or down.
The beeswarm plot provides an intuitive story: - Labor force status is the most powerful driver. Being “Not in the Labor Force” (yellow dots on the right) drastically increases the risk of poverty. - Education is the second key factor. Having a high school education or less strongly increases risk, whereas having “some college” or a bachelor’s degree strongly protects against poverty (purple dots on the left). - Age displays a non-linear relationship. Younger individuals have a higher risk, which gradually declines as they approach prime working age.
Interestingly, while being “Unemployed” is a massive shock that pushes risk sky-high, “Not in the Labor Force” has a broader, more consistent impact across the sample. This highlights a distinct form of vulnerability: people who have stopped looking for work are structurally more likely to be in poverty than those who are actively unemployed.

title: Blog10: Can Machine Learning Predict Poverty?
text:
Conclusion
This complete machine learning workflow yields three takeaways:

Predicting poverty is tractable, but the performance ceiling is modest. Complex models (XGBoost) outperform simple ones (AUC 0.765 vs 0.740), but the gain isn’t magical.
Predictive gains are practically valuable when used for targeting. The model successfully identifies a high-risk subgroup where poverty is 2.4 times more prevalent.
Interpretability tools like SHAP reveal structural truths. Structural detachment from the labor force, rather than temporary unemployment, is the strongest risk factor. Machine learning will not replace economists’ structural models, but it provides a powerful lens for identifying who needs help the most.

title: Blog10: Can Machine Learning Predict Poverty?
text:
Limitations
This analysis has several limitations:

Observational, not causal. The model identifies predictive correlations, not the causal effect of education or employment on poverty.
Limited features. The model relies on a small set of demographic and labor force variables. Adding geographic, health, or household structure data could improve predictive power.
Threshold-based evaluation. While Top-20% targeting reflects a realistic policy constraint, the optimal percentage might vary depending on the actual budget of the welfare program.


Data source: IPUMS CPS, Annual Social and Economic Supplement, 2024. Full code and data are available in the project repository.
